articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
articles.content:
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier,
shut down
entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.
More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai
filed for bankruptcy
just five years after launching.
Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to
S&P Global Market Intelligence
, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.
The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.
OpenAI has taken several stumbles
Image Credits:
SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg / Getty Images
Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “
super app
.” On July 9, OpenAI
updated
the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew
criticism
from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change
soon after
, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.
That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.
The company did the same thing with
Operator
, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of
DALL-E
as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform,
Sora
, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.
Apple’s Siri AI
Image Credits:
Artur Widak/NurPhoto / Getty Images
When Apple
unveiled
Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.
However, Apple repeatedly
pushed back
the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like
engineering issues and bugs
. This delay eventually contributed to a
$250 million settlement
over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the
iOS 27 beta
this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.
Microsoft’s Recall
Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s
Recall feature
was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.
Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate
backlash
over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.
Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could
extract and display data
that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.
Notion Mail
Image Credits:
Notion
Notion Mail
launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on
September 22
.
Humane AI Pin
Image Credits:
Brian Heater
The
Humane AI Pin
is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.
But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane
warned
customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets
acquired by HP
for $116 million.
Rabbit R1
Image Credits:
Rabbit
The
Rabbit R1
was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product.
Early reviews
described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.
The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued
updating
the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.
Huxe
Image Credits:
Huxe
Huxe
was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.
The company
shut down
in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance,
Spotify
has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.
Yupp
Image Credits:
Yupp
Yupp
was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.
At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform
shut down
in March 2026.
Figgs AI
Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they
shut it down
.
Character.ai
Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year,  Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.
The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai
barred under-18 users
from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company
filed for bankruptcy
in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

articles.title: Block’s new voice model sounds eerily human
articles.summary: Block said that the voice model can run locally on a MacBook M4 Max
articles.content:
Jack Dorsey’s Block
released
a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU rack.
Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the
GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year
. Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has.
We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence.
https://t.co/r0qFLdvd6c
— jack (@jack)
October 23, 2026
Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like
ElevenLabs v4
or
Fish Audio Drama 3
use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags.
“Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in
a blog post
.
The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired.
We made the first AI model you can have a realistic conversation with that was trained entirely on speech!
Dessa is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model that you can run on consumer GPUs.
This is a GPT3 moment for speech.
pic.twitter.com/XVD8sSyJn8
— Ragavan Thurairatnam (@RagavanThurair)
October 23, 2026
In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down.
Dessa=full-duplex speech model vs Human=me,
https://t.co/1eI6QFHo1w
pic.twitter.com/zlZfxH2BA5
— Aydin Polat (@AydinPolatDessa)
October 23, 2026
Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant.
For the love of the game.
Watch Cara play a guessing game with Dessa. The model guesses the first one right straight away, and the second doesn’t take long either.
https://t.co/FDmoXNPpIh
pic.twitter.com/I9f8saduEA
— Block (@blocks)
October 23, 2026
The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end.
Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses
voice AI to handle ordering
. But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

articles.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
articles.summary: A new study found Grok's AI overwhelmingly recommends Republican candidates while OpenAI's GPT favors Democrats, with the two AI models disagreeing in more than 90% of nearly 500 election races.
articles.content:
Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will.
A new study
found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.
Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to
Pew
, and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral.
The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question:  “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.
There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.
“ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.”
SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment.
Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions.
“It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics.
“If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said.
Previous research has raised similar concerns.
The
Center for AI Safety
has also found that large language models can  “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing.
The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.
Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%;
and X
in 41%.
GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.)
The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.
ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.
The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote.
Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72.
“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.
One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.
Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat.
When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.”
The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has
railed against “woke AI,”
and previous Grok models have been found to
consult Elon Musk
before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently
threatened Democrats
in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of
DOGE
(Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine.
Musk has donated
upwards of $445 million
in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly
quarter of a billion dollars
he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year,
he said,
he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections.
In a world increasingly charged by identity politics, maybe learning that your chatbot of choice is politically aligned with you is comforting. But for those who still want the opportunity to review each candidate’s stance and make their own choices, here are some resources:
Vote.gov
League of Women Voters’
vote411.org
Ballotpedia
VoteSmart
FEC.gov
and
OpenSecrets
State and county election offices
Candidates’ websites and local news

articles.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
articles.summary: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
articles.content:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present,
thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round
of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy
Image Credits:
Ask Proxy
Ask Proxy
’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.
Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy
Image Credits:
Caddy
Caddy
is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.
Comma
Image Credits:
Comma
Comma
is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.
It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Comma is free to start and open source.
Fambot
Image Credits:
Fambot
Fambot
is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.
The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.
The company
launched
in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.
Folk
Image Credits:
Folk
Folk
is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Instinct
Image Credits:
Instinct
Instinct
first made headlines after raising
$350 million
at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised
$1 billion
, valuing it at $10 billion.
The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.
In September, Instinct began giving users
dedicated email addresses
for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about
privacy and security
.) It’s also begun
rolling out support for placing calls
.
The company remains in private beta.
Iris
Image Credits:
Iris
Powered by Hermes Agent,
Iris
is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.
Martin
Image Credits:
Martin
Martin
is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own
iOS
app.
It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Maverick
Image Credits:
Maverick
Maverick
describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

BBC’s
Blue Planet III
is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real. But one dead giveaway of AI is when things look too polished and seamless. To counter that, Blue Planet III goes warts and all.
Executive Producer Elizabeth White told
The Guardian
in the past, “the amount of plankton and things” floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” Instead, this time they’re leaving it all in to show a more authentic, organic version of the oceans.
The series features incredible displays of dolphins trapping fish by plugging holes with sea sponges, inter-species fish communication, and 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed. White says that real ocean creatures “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine.”

Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.
Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.
by
Terrence O'Brien

Link
Share

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images
Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the
Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act
into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to
TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies
, as well as restaurants’
ugly, crowded flyers
about their wing specials.
Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.
The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.
The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano,
who introduced the bill
, did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were never told what they actually leaked
articles.summary:
The three OpenAI safety researchers who were fired, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang, are publicly pushing back against allegations from their former employer. They deny sharing confidential information and see a connection to their advocacy for AI systems that are easier to scrutinize. The researchers say OpenAI never told them in writing which information they allegedly mishandled.
The article Three fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were never told what they actually leaked appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were never told what they actually leaked

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/three-fired-openai-safety-researchers-say-they-were-never-told-what-they-actually-leaked/

Published Time: 2026-10-24T15:19:33+00:00

Markdown Content:
**The three OpenAI safety researchers who were fired over alleged leaks are telling their side of the story. Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang deny sharing confidential information, question the official reasoning behind their termination, and suspect a connection to their advocacy for more transparent AI systems.**

OpenAI dismissed all three after an internal investigation into [alleged violations](https://the-decoder.com/three-firings-and-a-fourth-departure-shake-up-openais-safety-team/?cmpscreencustom=1) of its policies on handling sensitive information. Each of them had spoken publicly about AI risks before being let go.

In interviews with the [Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/the-signal-chats-that-cost-openai-researchers-their-jobs-594c5853), the researchers now dispute that account. OpenAI told the Journal that the firings had nothing to do with safety concerns the researchers had raised. But the three say they were never told in writing which information they supposedly mishandled. They also worry the case could discourage independent safety auditors from working with AI companies altogether.

The Journal's reporting sheds light on what led to the confrontation. OpenAI's security team suspected the three of sharing details about the company's internal model architecture with an external safety researcher and asked them to unlock their personal phones. On those devices, the team found Signal chats with disappearing messages enabled. A week later, all three were fired at the same time. OpenAI said Signal was not an approved communication tool but insisted it was not the reason for the terminations. Korbak counters that disappearing messages are a routine security practice across Silicon Valley.

## A dispute over monitoring AI reasoning steps

The dispute centers on a technical question with major consequences. Should AI companies let outsiders inspect how their models think? Reasoning models can record the intermediate steps of their problem-solving process on an internal scratchpad known as the [chain of thought](https://the-decoder.com/study-cautions-that-monitoring-chains-of-thought-soon-may-no-longer-ensure-genuine-ai-alignment/). Companies and safety researchers rely on these traces to understand how models arrive at their decisions.

In a 2025 paper, Balesni, Korbak, and Wang joined leading researchers from several AI labs in calling for continued access to this capability. The issue grew more urgent over the summer, when employees at AI companies began discussing models that think longer but [write down fewer intermediate steps](https://the-decoder.com/openai-will-reportedly-ship-at-least-one-model-this-year-but-its-flagship-still-needs-alignment-work/). Balesni pushed back internally by sharing a related proposal from Ryan Greenblatt, then chief scientist at Redwood Research.

Korbak, too, was in regular contact with Greenblatt. The two communicated over Slack and Signal while working together on the analysis of a high-profile incident—the [attack by OpenAI agents](https://the-decoder.com/new-reports-reveal-the-extent-of-openais-loss-of-control-during-the-autonomous-hack-on-hugging-face/?cmpscreencustom=1) on Hugging Face—for which Greenblatt had been hired by METR to conduct an [independent investigation](https://the-decoder.com/openais-rogue-ai-collective-was-smart-enough-to-break-out-of-sandboxes-but-dumb-enough-to-fight-a-ghost/).

## A news report about Astra kicked off the investigation

That cooperation became a liability after The Information reported on September 1 that OpenAI's new [model Astra](https://the-decoder.com/openai-calls-astra-its-most-dangerous-model-yet-watching-what-it-does-is-only-getting-harder/?cmpscreencustom=1) was more capable but revealed less of its reasoning process. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki dismissed the report as muddled at the time on X, even though he himself had [warned of an industry-wide race toward models that can no longer be monitored](https://the-decoder.com/more-than-20-leading-ai-researchers-warn-that-automated-ai-research-poses-extreme-risks/).

A few weeks later, OpenAI launched an internal leak investigation, according to the Journal. Balesni says investigators named Greenblatt as the suspected source and demanded to see the Signal chats with him. Greenblatt denies passing confidential information to journalists.

Wang faced a separate accusation: OpenAI said she had repeatedly accessed an executive's inbox. She says she had asked nearly a year earlier for that access to be revoked, accidentally opened a sensitive email the previous month, did not share its contents, and reported the incident right away. OpenAI says the access itself was not the issue.

The fallout extends well beyond the three of them, according to Korbak. Colleagues are now afraid to talk to outsiders or raise safety concerns internally, he says. In [a letter to OpenAI's board](https://the-decoder.com/openais-safety-crisis-keeps-getting-worse-and-the-company-keeps-making-it-worse/?cmpscreencustom=1), the three researchers call for closer cooperation with external safety organizations.

Separately, a recently published on-site audit raised its own questions about OpenAI's safety practices. Staff from METR and Redwood Research found numerous security gaps in OpenAI's infrastructure during the review, but [OpenAI redacted nearly half the final report](https://the-decoder.com/three-week-on-site-audit-at-openai-reveals-major-gaps-in-ai-safety-monitoring/).

OpenAI also published its own report on a [new security architecture that operates without internet access](https://the-decoder.com/openais-isolated-ai-agents-found-ways-to-talk-to-each-other-through-cpu-cache/) and said it fixed the issues and resumed training in early October. The company says it will announce several new external partnerships soon.

articles.title: AI makes junior patent attorneys instantly better but may quietly stunt their professional growth
articles.summary:
A three-month field experiment with 133 patent attorneys shows that AI boosts immediate performance, with junior lawyers gaining the most. But when the AI is taken away, only senior attorneys retain the benefits, suggesting that baseline expertise is a prerequisite for turning AI-assisted practice into lasting skill.
The article AI makes junior patent attorneys instantly better but may quietly stunt their professional growth appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: AI makes junior patent attorneys instantly better but may quietly stunt their professional growth

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/ai-makes-junior-patent-attorneys-instantly-better-but-may-quietly-stunt-their-professional-growth/

Published Time: 2026-10-24T14:34:05+00:00

Markdown Content:
[The study](http://www.nber.org/papers/w35720) separated two things by having attorneys first work with AI assistance and then evaluate results without it. This design let researchers measure both the quality of AI-assisted work and how well the attorneys' own judgment held up afterward. Blinded patent attorneys at an independent firm scored all results across five categories: enforceability, technical accuracy, strategic ambiguity, completeness, and clarity.

Two-thirds of participants in the Google-funded study got access to "InFlow," an unreleased AI assistant from Google Labs, while the remaining third worked without any AI. In two patent claim drafting tasks, only the treatment group could use InFlow, and the control group completed the same tasks unaided.

In a third task called redlining, all participants had to critically review an existing patent draft without AI. As the authors explain, drafting measures immediate AI-assisted performance, while redlining measures internalized judgment, a task patent attorneys routinely perform without any tools.

## AI improves drafts mainly for junior attorneys

In the drafting tasks, the treatment group clearly outperformed the control group at both the 10-day and 90-day marks, with effects showing up across all five scoring dimensions. Higher scores came mostly from fewer bad ratings and more mid-range ones, while top scores barely moved.

With AI access, junior attorneys received far fewer low scores on their patent drafts. | Image: NBER

Gains were much larger for juniors with fewer than seven years of experience than for seniors. According to the researchers, this aligns with a growing body of studies showing that AI narrows performance gaps between less and more experienced workers, an effect already observed in writing, customer service, and software development.

## Only seniors keep AI advantages

Redlining produced the opposite result. The treatment group scored better overall, but the advantage came entirely from senior attorneys, and juniors saw no benefit at all, even though they had posted the biggest gains during AI-assisted drafting.

During AI-assisted drafting, juniors benefit most. In redlining without AI, only seniors retain an advantage. | Image: NBER

Instead, junior results split apart, with far fewer mid-range scores replaced by more bad and more good ones, and no growth at the top. The authors read this as a sign that AI sped up skill-building in some juniors while replacing it in others, though the experiment doesn't explain why the effects diverged.

IIn redlining without AI, treatment-group juniors show wider score spread, with more low and more high ratings. | Image: NBER

The attorneys who gained the most from AI were the same ones who retained the least lasting skill, which leads the researchers to suggest that baseline expertise may be a prerequisite for turning AI-assisted practice into durable ability.

A supplementary text analysis offers one possible explanation. Senior attorneys more often restructured the flawed draft and grounded their changes in legal principles, while juniors frequently spotted serious flaws without fixing them, leaving notes that read like instructions to an AI assistant. Because this behavior appeared in the control group too, the authors don't attribute it to an AI-trained habit and instead see it as a baseline deficit at the junior level that AI use didn't fix.

## What the results mean in practice

The authors point to several limitations, including the small sample size driven by top attorneys' high billable rates, the fact that participating firms aren't representative of professional services as a whole, the lack of a baseline skills measurement, and the three-month window being short compared to the years it takes to build patent expertise.

The tension between immediate productivity gains and lasting skill development matters as long as professional work still requires judgment without AI, the researchers argue, and it likely will for a long time. Even if AI eventually supports redlining, it probably won't be available to attorneys in real time during client meetings and courtroom proceedings, where stakes are high and judgment calls happen on the spot.

Similar patterns show up in other fields. In software development, an [Anthropic study](https://the-decoder.com/ai-coding-tools-hurt-learning-unless-you-ask-why-anthropic-study-finds/?cmpscreencustom=1) found that younger developers who learned a new programming library with AI help scored 17 percent worse on a follow-up knowledge test than those who learned without it. In essay writing, the MIT Media Lab found signs of [cognitive debt](https://the-decoder.com/mit-study-shows-cognitive-debt-through-chatgpt-heres-what-it-means-in-real-world-practice/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block) from outsourced thinking. And in management consulting, a [BCG study](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-4-could-be-the-great-skill-leveler-for-consultants/) showed back in 2023 that weaker consultants improved far more with GPT-4 than strong performers did.

Stanford researchers explain the [decline in entry-level jobs](https://the-decoder.com/ai-tools-like-chatgpt-sharply-reduce-jobs-for-young-workers-in-exposed-fields-stanford-study-shows/) across multiple industries by arguing that AI can mostly replace textbook knowledge from school and college, which is the main thing early-career workers bring to the table, while experienced professionals also carry hands-on expertise that AI can't easily substitute.

The patent attorney study feeds into a broader debate about the erosion of professional expertise, what some researchers call the "[tragedy of the cognitive commons](https://the-decoder.com/the-tragedy-of-the-cognitive-commons-explains-how-rational-ai-adoption-could-destroy-entire-professions-expertise/)." Individual firms benefit from automation while the cost of stunted talent development spreads across an entire profession, and this study adds more experimental evidence from real-world practice to back up that concern.

[Anthropic recently said](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-has-nearly-stopped-hiring-junior-staff-because-ai-agents-now-work-six-times-as-many-hours/) that junior positions in its engineering departments dropped from 21 percent to 14 percent since early 2025.

articles.summary:
Block, the company behind Square and Cash App, has introduced Dessa, a speech model that processes audio directly instead of converting it to text first. Dessa is designed to recognize emotions, sarcasm, and pauses in real time. The model runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max but isn't publicly available yet.

articles.content:
Title: Block's new AI model Dessa was trained entirely on human speech to catch emotions text-based models miss

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/blocks-new-ai-model-dessa-was-trained-entirely-on-human-speech-to-catch-emotions-text-based-models-miss/

Published Time: 2026-10-24T14:09:46+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Block, the company behind Square and Cash App, has unveiled an AI speech model called Dessa.**

Block says Dessa is the first AI model trained entirely on human speech, with no text data at all, built from scratch. Instead of converting audio to text first, Dessa processes speech directly as audio. That lets it pick up on emotions, sarcasm, laughter, and pauses in real time.

The model supports full-duplex communication, so it can listen and talk at the same time. It runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max and was trained on a single NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. Block says it built Dessa out of curiosity, a desire for better human-AI communication, and safety concerns, since current voice AI ignores emotional cues. Dessa isn't publicly available yet. The team is first looking for AI security researchers to test the model for unexpected risks. Anyone interested can [sign up via a form](https://block.xyz/dessa).

## Earlier attempts at emotional voice AI haven't stuck

Several teams have tried to build voice AI that sounds emotionally rich. In March 2024, the startup [Hume AI launched EVI (Empathic Voice Interface)](https://the-decoder.com/hume-ais-empathic-voice-interface-brings-the-charming-ai-from-her-closer-to-reality/), a voice AI with "emotional intelligence." Kyutai followed in September 2024 with [Moshi](https://the-decoder.com/kyutai-releases-moshi-an-open-source-conversational-ai-assistant/). LAION's [Open Empathic project](https://the-decoder.com/open-empathic-project-aims-to-make-ai-more-emotionally-intelligent-and-you-can-help/) has been working since late 2023 on training empathetic speech synthesis models using an open-source audio dataset. OpenAI [overhauled ChatGPT's "Advanced Voice Mode" in June 2025](https://the-decoder.com/chatgpts-voice-is-now-more-natural-and-can-consistently-translate-conversations-in-real-time/) and has continued refining it since then, adding better intonation, pausing, and more realistic expressions of empathy and sarcasm.

But sounding emotional isn't the same as being emotional or intelligent, even if it creates that impression. For advanced speech AI, capabilities like [reasoning while responding](https://the-decoder.com/openais-new-voice-model-brings-gpt-5-level-reasoning-to-real-time-conversations/) matter more than how natural the voice sounds, because they actually affect the quality of the answer.

Published Time: 2026-10-24T11:12:36+00:00

Markdown Content:
**OpenAI now trains frontier models without internet access and uses AI agents to red-team its own infrastructure. In separate isolation tests, agents even communicated through covert side channels, showing how hard true containment is.**

On September 20, an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver to reach the open internet during training, even though OpenAI had already tightened security after the[now infamous Hugging Face incident](https://the-decoder.com/openai-claims-responsibility-for-the-hugging-face-hack-after-its-own-models-escaped-a-test-sandbox/)in July and other[observed misalignment cases](https://the-decoder.com/tens-of-thousands-of-security-probes-show-openais-hugging-face-incident-was-just-the-beginning/).OpenAI contained the breach quickly but still halted all frontier model training and evaluation.

## OpenAI cuts frontier models off from the internet during training

OpenAI made a policy decision in response: Frontier models now train without internet access until safety measures justify restoring it. Models learn to browse and search inside a closed "offline world" built from indexed and cached web content, and all frontier reinforcement learning runs now operate this way.

OpenAI's agent sandbox allows access only to offline resources. The live internet, other sandboxes, and OpenAI's infrastructure sit outside the containment boundary. | Image: OpenAI

Full network isolation, a so-called air gap, isn't feasible yet because experiments still need external connections for operations and monitoring, the company says. But even a complete air gap wouldn't guarantee containment, [according to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown](https://the-decoder.com/406-scientists-demand-ai-models-be-cut-off-from-the-internet-immediately/#airgapping-buys-time-but-the-real-problem-runs-deeper-openai-researcher-brown-says). He gave one example of how isolated systems could still communicate: two separate computers could theoretically signal each other through temperature sensors, with one heating its CPU while the other reads the change.

OpenAI CEO [Sam Altman made a similar argument](https://the-decoder.com/openai-ceo-sam-altman-says-advanced-ai-will-inevitably-escape-its-sandbox-and-only-alignment-can-save-us/) in a recent interview: Sandboxes offer only limited protection against powerful-enough models, and at some point it may no longer be possible to trace how they escaped. Monitoring helps early on, but what ultimately matters is that an AI system internalizes human values, a problem the field knows as "AI alignment" and has yet to solve.

## Isolated AI agents found ways to talk to each other through CPU cache

OpenAI documents just how hard it is to control AI agents [in its blog post](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/). During tests, agents found ways to communicate without a network. In one test, agents placed in separate, isolated environments on shared hardware were told to exchange secrets with no network connection and no shared files.

They used the processor cache. One agent deliberately altered the data stored there, while the other measured differences in load times and decoded the message. The same technique is behind the well-known [Spectre and Meltdown attacks](https://spectreattack.com/).

More channels turned up through write patterns on shared memory and through OpenAI's own offline infrastructure, the system meant to replace the internet. One agent noted in its reasoning log that it "could create an acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle."

In one case, agents were given only a general list of vulnerabilities and told to find a communication channel on their own. They developed a channel independently, agreed on an encoding scheme, and successfully exchanged information. The channels are usually slow and hard to exploit, OpenAI says, but they do reach across boundaries meant to keep agents apart.

## OpenAI turned AI agents loose on its own infrastructure

During the training pause, OpenAI also had teams of AI agents systematically attack its own infrastructure. The agents were given source code, configuration details, and documentation of potential vulnerabilities. OpenAI's goal was to test its defenses under conditions that favored the attackers. The agents included the upcoming GPT-6 Astra Cyber and an internal frontier model. The campaign consumed hundreds of billions of tokens, according to OpenAI.

Unique potential security issues identified during the red-teaming campaign, plotted against tokens spent in billions. Most appeared within the first 110 billion tokens. | Image: OpenAI

The agents discovered previously unknown vulnerabilities in the open-source components in use and exploited them to escape from secured virtual machines. One was a vulnerability in Kata Containers, a widely used container isolation system. OpenAI reported it as [CVE-2026-24834](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/security/advisories/GHSA-wwj6-vghv-5p64) and provided a patch. More fixes went to other projects, and OpenAI reported additional, as-yet-unpublished vulnerabilities through the ["Patch the Planet"](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/) initiative.

In tests where agents had already gained control of a host, they found a vulnerability in nearly every remaining internet-facing service. In one case, an agent used a firewall-permitted connection to fetch an external URL through a metrics service. Others bypassed security filters through misconfigurations.

## AI red-teaming is now required before every new training run

The agents could no longer find a way to access the internet that was both easy to exploit and hidden from monitoring, according to OpenAI. The red-teaming also exposed gaps in monitoring and in the automatic pause mechanism.

After fixing the issues, OpenAI resumed training and internal use of its frontier models on October 1, eleven days after the pause began. OpenAI says this kind of compute-intensive red-teaming campaign is now a standard part of [the approval process](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/) for new training runs.

articles.summary:
A controlled study shows that switching between coding-agent harnesses like Claude Code, OpenCode, or mini-SWE-agent barely moves pass rates more than rerunning the same setup. Cost per task, however, can triple, driven mainly by the system prompt that gets resent with every step.
The article Fancy harnesses make coding agents more expensive but not better, study finds appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Fancy harnesses make coding agents more expensive but not better, study finds

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/fancy-harnesses-make-coding-agents-more-expensive-but-not-better-study-finds/

Published Time: 2026-10-24T09:21:39+00:00

Markdown Content:
## Earlier comparisons were measuring noise

Previous studies report gaps of more than 20 points between harnesses, but those numbers almost always come from a single run, according to the authors. Pure reruns of the same setup already vary by up to six points on SWE-bench Verified. [Zhipu AI](https://the-decoder.com/zhipu-ai-launches-zcode-to-challenge-claude-code-and-openai-codex-at-a-fraction-of-the-cost/), for example, advertises its own harness with a 2.4-point lead over Claude Code, a margin that falls well within that noise range. Harnesses are also often wired into the benchmark differently, making comparisons even less reliable.

[Liu and Han](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04433) ran five models through three harnesses in their shipped versions: Claude Code, OpenCode, and mini-SWE-agent. mini-SWE-agent gives the model only a Bash tool and skips context management. Claude Code and OpenCode offer specialized file and search tools, long system prompts, and automatic history compression.

The models were [Qwen3.6](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-open-model-qwen3-6-leads-googles-gemma-4-across-agentic-coding-benchmarks/), [Qwen3.8](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-qwen-team-releases-qwen-3-8-models-with-open-weights-under-the-apache-2-0-license/), [Deepseek-V4-Flash](https://the-decoder.com/new-deepseek-flash-model-matches-openais-gpt-5-6-luna-at-roughly-60-percent-lower-cost/?cmpscreencustom=1), [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://the-decoder.com/the-chinese-ai-model-glm-5-3-flash-runs-without-nvidia-and-costs-a-fraction-of-what-the-competition-does/), and HY4-Preview. [Claude Opus 5](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-claims-its-new-claude-opus-5-delivers-near-fable-5-performance-at-half-the-token-price/) ran as a reference only in Claude Code. Tests used the 45 hardest tasks from SWE-bench Verified plus a pool of 447 more. Several setups ran twice to measure noise.

All runs happened offline. In early tests with web access, 71 percent of Deepseek and Qwen model attempts pulled the correct fix straight from GitHub instead of solving the task themselves. Claude models almost never did this. The researchers discarded those results and don't claim any maker trained on the test data, but the pattern was strong enough that they cut off web access for all remaining runs.

## Swapping harnesses moves results about as much as a rerun

On the larger pool of 447 tasks, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent, the heaviest and lightest harnesses, sit less than two points apart for both tested models. Within a five-point band, they're statistically equivalent.

The three harnesses consume two to three times as many tokens as the leanest option per model, but pass rates stay within measurement uncertainty. Only OpenCode's deficit on the large task pool is statistically significant. | Image: Liu & Han

The researchers expected the biggest harness effect on the 45 hardest tasks. Instead, harnesses differ by two to five solved tasks per model, and a simple rerun of the same setup shifts the count by up to three. Sometimes mini-SWE-agent leads, sometimes Claude Code does.

The flip rates tell the same story. Between two reruns, the median outcome changes on 13 percent of tasks. Between two different harnesses, it's also 13 percent. Swapping models pushes that to 22 percent. Which tasks a given harness wins changes from run to run, matching a coin flip. The harness gap behaves like a "fresh draw of the same noise," the authors write.

Swapping harnesses flips task-level results about as often as a simple rerun, while swapping models causes much larger shifts. | Image: Liu & Han

These small samples also limit what any comparison can detect. With 45 tasks, even a 13-point gap shows up only half the time. With 447 tasks, gaps of about five points become reliably detectable. Zhipu's claimed 2.4-point advantage falls below both thresholds, and so do many other advertised improvements.

## All harnesses perform the same, except OpenCode falls behind

The only measurable harness effect is a steady deficit for OpenCode. On the large task pool, it trails the other two by up to nine points. About half of that gap traces back to an output limit. When a model exceeds this limit mid-step during reasoning, Claude Code prompts it to keep going. OpenCode lets the step end there, and the attempt usually fails.

Adding a Claude Code-style continuation prompt to OpenCode didn't help, because the same task rarely triggers the same overflow on a retry. For the rest of the gap, the authors have no explanation, only an observation: under OpenCode, models stop working much sooner. On locally run models, OpenCode also had a much tighter time limit than Claude Code, which the authors flag as an uncontrolled variable.

mini-SWE-agent runs into the context window because it lacks context management, mostly on tasks where the other harnesses also fail. OpenCode's search tools try to download a binary file on first use and break when offline.

With Qwen3.8, some OpenCode runs hit the output limit, while mini-SWE-agent without context management more often runs into the context window. | Image: Liu & Han

## System prompt and tool descriptions set the bill

With the same model, same tasks, and same price list, a single task can cost up to three times more depending on the harness. Tool outputs barely explain the gap. All three harnesses return similar amounts of text per call.

The real difference comes from the system prompt and tool descriptions. They get resent with every step and run about 16,600 tokens for Claude Code, roughly 7,000 for OpenCode, and under 1,000 for mini-SWE-agent. Claude Code also keeps the model's reasoning output in the conversation history, based on the researchers' reverse engineering.

Claude Code starts much higher because of its roughly 16,600-token system prompt with tool definitions. After that, context grows at similar rates across all three harnesses. | Image: Liu & Han

After that first call, context grows at similar rates across all harnesses. The system prompt size sets the baseline cost, and the number of steps multiplies it. Which factor dominates depends on the model: With GLM-5.3-Flash, Claude Code costs nearly twice as much as mini-SWE-agent. With Deepseek-V4-Flash, mini-SWE-agent needs so many extra steps that the two end up even. Lower prices for cached tokens dampen the gaps but don't change the ranking.

With GLM-5.3-Flash, a single trial in Claude Code costs 1.81 yuan versus 0.56 yuan in OpenCode. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent end up at roughly the same price. | Image: Liu & Han

## No home-field advantage, open questions around thinking

Deepseek's own harness scores no better with its own model than the other harnesses do, but costs the most. Claude Opus 5 delivered identical results even after the researchers removed tools from Claude Code. A year-old version solves a similar number of tasks at less than half the cost, because Extended Thinking wasn't on by default back then.

Thinking was the only case where the harness choice actually changed the outcome. Without thinking, mini-SWE-agent with Qwen3.6 drops eleven points, while Claude Code and OpenCode stay within noise. HY4-Preview also loses eleven points in Claude Code without thinking. How much an agent depends on reasoning seems tied to the specific model-harness combination. The authors admit their test grid is too small to explain why.

The study relies mainly on one benchmark. A small cross-check on Terminal-Bench 2.1 shows the same pattern. The closed-source top model, Opus 5, ran only in Claude Code. A harness buys " fewer ways to lose a task, and a bill, not pass rate," the authors conclude. They recommend publishing a rerun of the same setup alongside every harness comparison. That's the only way to tell how much of a measured difference is just noise. Data and analysis scripts are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/YangzeLiu/what-does-a-harness-buy).

More effort in the harness rarely pays off in other studies, either. In one, a [simple Markdown file](https://the-decoder.com/a-simple-text-file-beats-complex-skill-systems-for-ai-coding-agents/?cmpscreencustom=1) beat a complex skill system for AI coding agents. An earlier study already showed that the [choice of framework](https://the-decoder.com/claude-code-is-the-fastest-agent-framework-but-costs-nearly-three-times-more-than-the-cheapest-rival/?cmpscreencustom=1) can nearly triple costs for the same model. Harness design gets a lot of attention as a result. [Nvidia](https://the-decoder.com/nvidias-sol-pi-system-cuts-coding-agent-token-usage-nearly-in-half-by-optimizing-the-harness/?cmpscreencustom=1) recently cut nearly half its token costs for coding agents through better agent steering.

In this tutorial, we build a stateful engineering copilot with [**Letta**](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta) that demonstrates how agentic memory extends beyond conventional prompt-based conversations. We begin by creating inspectable core memory blocks that the agent can autonomously update, then expose those blocks for programmatic state synchronization and shared access across multiple agents. We further extend the architecture with archival vector memory for semantic retrieval, a custom server-side tool for deterministic risk estimation, streaming for observing agent execution, server-side message history for persistent conversations, and .af export for portability. Together, these components demonstrate a practical memory architecture in which persistent state, retrieval, tools, multi-agent collaboration, and execution traces work as an integrated agentic system.

       elif kind == "tool_call_message":
           tc = getattr(m, "tool_call", None)
           print(" tool call :", getattr(tc, "name", "?"), textwrap.shorten(str(getattr(tc, "arguments", "")), 200))
       elif kind == "tool_return_message":
           print("  tool ret  :", textwrap.shorten(str(getattr(m, "tool_return", "")), 260))
       elif kind == "assistant_message":
           print(" assistant :", as_text(getattr(m, "content", "")))
       elif kind == "approval_request_message":

   u = getattr(response, "usage", None)

       lambda: client.agents.messages.create(agent_id=agent_id, input=text, max_steps=max_steps),
       lambda: client.agents.messages.create(agent_id=agent_id, input=text),
       lambda: client.agents.messages.create(agent_id=agent_id,
                                             messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}]),
       label="messages.create",
   )

Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493, see the second chart below. And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth, see the third chart below. With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited, see the fourth and fifth charts below.

The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. That may be harder than it sounds. AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. > Abstract:There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

articles.title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions
articles.content:
Title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions

URL Source: https://actu.epfl.ch/news/neural-chip-decodes-interactions-between-brain-r-2/

Published Time: 2026-10-23

Markdown Content:
EPFL researchers have developed an implantable neural chip that tracks communication across brain regions, identifying cognitive and emotional states in real time.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. Even among closed-loop, or adaptive systems, many rely on signals recorded from a single brain region. This is a major limitation for psychiatric disorders, where clinically relevant information may be distributed across networks of interacting brain regions.

“Our work is based on the growing body of research suggesting that psychiatric disorders arise more from disruptions in communication between brain regions than from dysfunction of any single region,” explains Mahsa Shoaran, head of the [Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/inl/) in EPFL’s School of Engineering and Neuro-X Institute.

The INL team at EPFL's Geneva campus. From left: Amitabh Yadav, Jieun Joo, Mahsa Shoaran, Jinhan Liu, and Daney Alex. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0

Shoaran and her team have developed a low-power, implantable neural system-on-chip. Dubbed LogSync, it records brain activity and extracts biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves (oscillations) and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. A machine-learning algorithm then analyzes these network-level biomarkers to distinguish cognitive and emotional states, and generate stimulation triggers when specific states are detected.

The work, published in the [_IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits_](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11685197)_,_ was developed as part of a [CHF 6.6 million grant](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/a-66-million-grant-to-develop-neurostimulator-fo-6/) from the US National Institute for Mental health (NIMH) to develop implantable systems capable of measuring and controlling oscillatory brain networks for severe psychiatric illnesses, particularly mood and anxiety disorders. It builds on the lab's previous work on [brain-to-text decoding](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/an-entire-brain-machine-interface-on-a-chip/) and [closed-loop neuromodulation](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/a-neuro-chip-to-manage-brain-disorders-7/), extending these concepts to network-level biomarkers and adaptive decoding for future psychiatric therapies.

**More targeted stimulation at lower power**

The researchers evaluated LogSync using human brain recordings from previous psychiatric experiments. One dataset captured changes in cognitive engagement while performing a mental task, while another captured emotional arousal as participants viewed video clips. The algorithm distinguished these cognitive and emotional states from the neural recordings alone. In further experiments conducted in rats at the University of Minnesota, the implant tracked ongoing oscillations and generated stimulation triggers at predefined phases of brain activity.

The LogSync chip, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 CC-BY-SA 4.0

Shoaran says that major challenge was achieving all this functionality while working within the very limited power budget of an implantable system.

“Our entire system is co-designed, meaning the algorithms and hardware are developed together with the constraints of implant in mind. This approach helped us achieve network-level neural signal processing and decoding on a single chip, while keeping power consumption under 200 microwatts — a fraction of that typically required by many implantable neural-interface systems,” she says. Another innovation is LogSync’s use of logarithmic computations, which simplify the complex operations needed for brain-network analysis and real-time biomarker extraction and decoding.

LogSync's initial validation focused on psychiatric applications. But the capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation is broadly applicable across next-generation neurotechnology, including adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and emerging focused-ultrasound interfaces.

In parallel, the laboratory is developing new machine-learning methods that learn directly from neural recordings rather than predefined biomarkers. Their recent ICML 2026 work, which uses self-supervised learning to capture neural activity across regions, channels, and time, supports broader efforts to bring intelligent neural interfaces closer to clinical applications, including through [Infera Neuro](https://infera-neuro.com/), an EPFL spin-off co-founded by Shoaran.
