articles.title: America Has Lost 200k of Jobs in Media, Film and the Arts. How Much Is AI?
articles.content:
Title: AI and the Fall? of the Creative Class

URL Source: https://www.apricitas.io/p/ai-and-the-fall-of-the-creative-class

Published Time: 2026-09-27T14:01:59+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Thanks for reading! If you haven’t subscribed, please click the button below:**

**By subscribing, you’ll join over 80,000 people who read Apricitas!**

America has lost more than 200k jobs in “creative” industries over the last four years, with roughly 50k lost within the last year alone. That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history, with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008. Yet there’s no generalized recession today—instead, this period of job loss coincides with the rise of AI systems that can compose wholesale novels, photorealistic images, soundalike music, and practically every other form of digital art, en masse and at extremely low costs. Is this the fall of the Creative Class?

Proving the exact amount of AI-driven job loss in the arts is extremely difficult. Media firms are decidedly coy about their AI use, both to protect against public backlash and, more financially important, to preserve the legal basis for their copyrights. The effects of AI are also hard to disentangle from other factors currently affecting arts businesses, like consolidation in Hollywood, offshoring of content production, or the continued displacement of traditional media providers in favor of social media creators. Yet perhaps the clearest evidence of AI’s influence is just that all subsectors of the digital arts industry are losing jobs, while in-person entertainment is still growing at a healthy pace.

Some of those digital job losses are just a continuation of prior trends, like in the publishing industry where technological change has been continually grinding away newspaper and magazine jobs for decades. Yet for sectors like live broadcasting, streaming, or graphic design, recent experience is an unusual downturn compared to the tranquility of years prior. Then there’s the worst-hit sector, movie & sound recording, which has been bleeding jobs at a nearly unprecedented pace over the last three years.

Hollywood has never seen a stretch as bad as the last four years, with the movie & TV industry losing more than 100k jobs, nearly one-third of the sector’s total. At the depths touched this summer, total employment was lower than at any point since the 2008 recession and approaching the lowest point in 30 years. The streaming era has proven an extremely difficult transition, with traditional films and TV shows losing watch time to user-generated and increasingly AI-assisted or AI-generated content flows.

Overall, nearly half the media job losses of the last four years have been concentrated in the movie & sound recording sector that includes Hollywood. Written publishing has been the next-largest source of job loss, with employment down by more than 70k over the same time frame. Yet the job losses have by no means been contained to any particular part of media; instead they’ve hit nearly every subsector at some point. Nor do they show any sign of abating, with losses consistently hovering at around 50k per year and even accelerating in recent months. Will further AI development continue displacing workers in creative industries?

To understand what **could**happen to the business of art amidst the rise of AI, it’s important to understand what **did** happen to it during the first digital transition, the rise of the internet.

It was the turn of the millennium, and _Metallica_ had a problem. Demos of their upcoming, unreleased tracks were bouncing around radio and the internet, originally leaked onto a new internet file-sharing website called Napster. There they found thousands of files shared amongst hundreds of thousands of users, many of which were direct rips of albums that sold for $15 being offered for free. The most anticipated albums were often leaked online even before they were on store shelves. _Metallica_ sued Napster for copyright infringement, and they were soon joined by separate suits from other prominent artists and eventually the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).

Much of the general public was understandably unsympathetic to _Metallica_, perceived as a bunch of already-successful millionaires trying to bilk even more money from listeners, and were even less sympathetic towards the RIAA, perceived as scurrilous middlemen who take from artists and fans alike. But the two of them easily won their lawsuit, forcing Napster into bankruptcy. Yet _Metallica_ may have been right on the law but were on the wrong side of technology; the RIAA had won the battle but was losing the war.

The modern internet made file-sharing extremely easy, and no matter how much whac-a-mole companies played, they could not possibly catch every illegal upload. The perennial threat of piracy undermined their copyright and limited their ability to charge for music. Eventually, the value of individual songs fell to the point that companies like Spotify and Apple Music could swoop in to acquire massive catalogues, consolidate them, and charge a comparatively trivial fee for access. For what a single _Metallica_ album would have cost in 2000, you can now get a month’s worth of unlimited access to nearly all human-made music.

The music industry has never returned to the heyday paydays of the peak CD era—even without adjusting for inflation, streaming revenue pales in comparison to ‘90s physical media sales. This was a massive boon to consumers, but it was also a squeeze on musicians that forced them to fundamentally change their business model over time. Instead of just selling records to earn money directly, music itself increasingly became a loss-leading advertisement for the live concerts (and merch) that provided a growing share of artists’ income. Tours got longer, venues got bigger, ticket prices skyrocketed, and musicians frequently took on roles closer to public influencers than isolated artistes. Were it not for rising concert sales, the business model of music would have completely collapsed, and the income going to musicians would have cratered.

Of course, there were still significant downsides to the transition into the streaming era. Bands (especially smaller ones) complain about the unending pressure to always be on tour. Musicians whose content was suited to home listening lost out to those more suited to giant festivals. Even accounting for concert revenues, musicians made less money than before. Yet musicians fared better than many areas of entertainment subsectors because there was a live component to fall back on—for many media industries, the digital era left no such comfort.

Over time, the business of video has moved in the opposite direction of music—out of the theatre and into the home. Hollywood formerly made most of its money enticing customers to visit sold-out movie theatres, but these were gradually supplanted by broadcast TV, cable, and physical media. Yet because each successful technological leap increased total video watch time, the industry was still able to thrive amidst technological upheaval. That is, until the modern streaming era.

Today, the plethora of video options and the rise of social media have sent video producers into a vicious competition for limited attention. Even before adjusting for inflation, movie ticket sales ended last year down 25% from their 2019 peak, cable revenue is down 18% from its peak, and streaming revenue has not been able to compensate for the drop. The mountain of free user-generated content on YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, or social media was already presenting harsh competition for traditional video companies in the years before ChatGPT’s launch, and now streaming services are also competing with a flood of AI-generated content. The business model of video media is fundamentally getting squeezed, and unlike in the music industry, there’s basically no equivalent to live concerts that Hollywood can be used to ease the pain.

The actual worst-case scenario for creative workers amidst the AI revolution is something similar to what happened to the publishing industry after the advent of the internet—that is, near-total collapse of their fundamental business model. Newspapers used to employ roughly half a million people in the US, more than the entire oil industry, and now their payrolls are down nearly 85% and still dropping. Magazine publishers likewise have let 66% of their staff go since the 90s, while book publishers have lost 40%.

The routine informational updates that previously formed newspapers’ bread-and-butter were all de-bundled—box scores moved to sports websites, stock movements went to financial websites, forecasts went to weather websites—each loss compounding on itself to undermine consumers’ need to buy the paper. Search engines became the first place people looked to for information, and newspapers’ advertising revenue rapidly started flowing to companies like Google instead. The collective of social media users became faster at breaking any news story than a daily paper could ever hope to be. When papers eventually did start aggressively paywalling content, the internet made it trivially easy for people to just copy the articles’ content and share it beyond the paywall. The entire business model had collapsed, to the point that now only a select few major newspapers can even survive.

That scale of copyright dilution and forced unbundling is the worst-case scenario for media businesses in the age of AI. It’s possible arts jobs could survive via consumers’ deep-seated aversion to explicitly AI-generated content, but AI is increasingly being used throughout media in ways invisible to the average end consumer. [Roughly 32% of workers in the overall arts, entertainment, and recreation sector use Generative AI to some extent](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=1Z2RG), which is [less than the 62% average across all industries](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=1XQ3Q), but still enough that virtually every major media project could have some AI within its workflow.

Indeed, AI is likely seeping into media production processes in ways large companies themselves would struggle to prevent even when they desire to—how can a TV studio be sure nobody in their writers’ room is consulting ChatGPT for jokes or any storyboard artist is generating concept art? And even if professional TV and movie studios do effectively hold out against temptation and prevent internal AI use, how long can they compete with the large mass of wannabe independent creators with much fewer scruples? Plenty of media businesses tried to hold out against the algorithmic content waves of the 2010s and were buried as a result.

Yet fundamentally, it’s difficult to meaningfully predict how new technologies will interact with existing arts businesses. Take the unexpected resurgence in book sales over the last four years. The novel as a commercial art form had been struggling for decades, with fewer books sold in 2019 than at the beginning of the millennium, but the last six years have seen an unprecedented 70% surge in sales. The unlikely savior of the printed word came from perhaps its polar opposite—TikTok.

Of course, fewer people read now than ever before—for the general public, short-form video apps have accelerated the displacement of reading, just as TV, video games, or social media before them. Yet for a dwindling number of dedicated repeat readers, “BookTok” became a new way to source reviews, analysis, discourse, and community in a way that boosted the reading experience and absolutely turbocharged book sales. It’s possible that AI tools could have those same totally unpredictable spillovers for other museums, concerts, or other forms of art in ways that are unpredictable today, in much the same way short-form video saved books in ways that

24 October, 2026 in [advertising](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/category/non-technical/advertising/) | Tags: [Abhinav Nellore](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/tag/abhinav-nellore/), [Johannes Schmitt](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/tag/johannes-schmitt/), [Rachel Ward](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/tag/rachel-ward/), [Soledad Villar](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/tag/soledad-villar/) | by [Terence Tao](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/author/teorth/)

_[This is a guest post by [Abhinav Nellore](https://www.ohsu.edu/people/abhinav-nellore-phd), [Johannes Schmitt](https://johannesschmitt.gitlab.io/), [Soledad Villar](https://www.ams.jhu.edu/villar/), and [Rachel Ward](https://oden.utexas.edu/people/directory/rachel--ward/) – T.]_

OpenAI’s math write-ups at [https://github.com/openai/math](https://github.com/openai/math) can be difficult to understand and can have incomplete citations.

[https://github.com/mathcommunity/oai-math-revised/](https://github.com/mathcommunity/oai-math-revised/)seeks to be an inclusive effort to improve these write-ups, and the broader math community–students, postdocs, professors, and enthusiasts–is invited to participate.

The repo is browsable at [https://mathcommunity.github.io/oai-math-revised/](https://mathcommunity.github.io/oai-math-revised/)

We also invite the community to email [mathcommunityadmin@gmail.com](mailto:mathcommunityadmin@gmail.com) if they want to serve as admins/reviewers and for which categories from [https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/overview.pdf](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/overview.pdf) they’d be appropriate for reviews.

articles.content:
Title: Argus — Free, Open-Source AI Security Operations Platform | Thomas Unise

URL Source: https://thomasunise.com/argus

Markdown Content:
Open Source Free · MIT Licensed Self-Hosted

## Attackers have AI agents now. So do you.

Argus is a free, open-source security operations platform that watches your cloud, logins, code and devices around the clock, catches machine-speed attacks the moment they start, and shuts them down in seconds. AI does the legwork. Guardrails you control decide what it's allowed to touch.

Seconds, not hours From detection to a blocked attacker, with autonomous response on

27 one-click fixes Across AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Okta, Entra, CrowdStrike and more

$0 license No seats, no usage fees, no lock-in. You own all of it

A stolen key handed to an AI agent can fire sixty probing calls across twenty of your cloud services in less time than it takes to read this sentence. Swarms of fake identities can spray passwords at your admin accounts from a hundred places at once. By the time a person reads the first alert, the attacker has already moved on to the next system.

Most security tools were built for attackers who sleep. Argus was built for the ones that don't. It watches at machine speed, investigates at machine speed, and when you let it, responds at machine speed. It does all of that through one broker with approvals, dry runs, automatic rollback and a kill switch, so speed never turns into a new risk.

> Fast enough to stop an AI attacker. Disciplined enough to trust with your production systems.

01 / See it all

Every asset, every login, one map

Argus pulls in your AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, GitHub, Okta, Entra, devices and network traffic and links them into one evidence graph. You see the attack paths before an attacker does.

02 / Catch it early

Built to spot AI-driven attacks

Detections for agent swarms, machine-speed recon, privilege escalation, public exposure, leaked secrets and rogue workloads. Tripwires bait attackers' AI agents into revealing themselves.

03 / Shut it down

Respond in seconds, from Slack

Block an IP, contain a laptop through CrowdStrike or SentinelOne, disable a user, lock down a public bucket. Approve, deny or roll back with one tap in Slack, or let a playbook do it for you.

04 / Rein in AI

Stop shadow AI and data leaks

Find every AI tool your team is quietly using. Route your apps' and team's OpenAI and Anthropic calls through one gateway with approved models, data-loss rules, budgets and a full usage log.

05 / Know you're covered

Test your defenses on demand

Replay eight AI-agent attacks in a sealed sandbox and get a report of exactly what you'd catch and what would slip through. Let autonomous pentesting probe your own systems, inside the scope you set.

06 / Prove it

Audit-ready from day one

Every action is signed into a tamper-evident audit trail stored in write-once storage. Control mapping for SOC 2, NIST 800-171 and ISO 27001 is built in.

1.   02:14:07 Attacker An attacker's AI agent finds what looks like an LLM API key in your code and tries to use it.The key is a canary that Argus planted. Nothing real was exposed.Tripwire
2.   02:14:08 Detect Argus raises a high-severity detection with the attacker's source address and the full evidence trail.Caught
3.   02:14:09 Respond Your playbook blocks the source at your Cloudflare firewall, within the hourly cap you set.Policy, deny-lists and the kill switch are checked first, every time.Blocked
4.   02:14:10 Notify Slack lights up with what happened, why, and a one-tap Roll back button.Slack
5.   07:30:00 Review Your team starts the day with a closed incident, a signed audit record and a choice: keep the block, or let it expire.If nobody keeps it, Argus rolls the block back automatically when its timer runs out.Done

Letting software act on its own in production is a big decision, so Argus makes it a small, reversible one. The AI agents never touch your systems directly. They investigate with read-only access and can only propose. Every change, whether a person asks for it, an agent suggests it or a playbook fires, passes through the same broker.

Off until you say so Autonomous response and autonomous pentesting ship switched off, and each needs both a deployment switch and a per-tenant opt-in.

Shadow mode first Playbooks start by logging what they would have done, so you see their judgment before you give them the keys.

Reversible only Autonomous playbooks run reversible actions, and each one rolls back automatically unless someone decides to keep it.

Capped Hourly limits per tenant and per playbook, a blast-radius limit, and two human approvals for high-risk actions.

One switch The kill switch stops every action in a tenant or across the whole deployment instantly.

Hard to fool Everything the AI reads is treated as untrusted, and the agents are tested against prompt-injection attacks.

Autonomous response

### Threats handled while you sleep

Playbooks turn a detection into a fix with no human in the loop, then undo it on a timer unless you keep it. Approve, deny and roll back from Slack buttons.

AI gateway

### One front door for every AI call

Your team uses OpenAI and Anthropic with company-held keys, approved models, data-loss rules, budgets and prompt-injection flags. Staff get Argus keys; your real provider keys stay locked inside Argus.

Shadow-AI discovery

### See which AI tools your staff really use

Argus spots AI services in your network traffic, cloud accounts and SSO grants, keeps an inventory, and raises an alert for anything unreviewed or blocked.

Attack simulator

### A fire drill for AI-driven attacks

Eight realistic agent attacks, from credential-spray swarms to a rogue Kubernetes agent, replayed in a sealed sandbox. Add "slow and low" evasion variants to find the gaps attackers would exploit.

Autonomous pentesting

### A red team that never clocks out

An AI planner picks the tests, Argus runs them through scanners like Nuclei, ZAP and Trivy, then plans the next round from what it found. It stays inside your authorized scope, re-checked before every step.

Threat intel

### Fix what's actually being exploited

Every vulnerability is checked against the CISA Known Exploited list and scored for exploit likelihood. Anything attackers are actively using jumps to the top of your queue.

AI-agent canaries

### Traps built for AI attackers

Fake LLM keys, fake MCP servers, decoy agent rules files and planted prompt injections. An agent that bites gives itself away instantly.

Endpoint containment

### Isolate a compromised laptop in one step

New CrowdStrike and SentinelOne actions contain a device straight from Argus, with the same approvals, dry run and rollback as everything else.

MIT licensed Self-hosted Claude, OpenAI, local Ollama or no AI at all Docker, Helm, Terraform for AWS and Azure

quickstart

```
$ git clone https://github.com/thomasunise/argus.git && cd argus
$ python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
$ pip install -r requirements.txt
$ cp .env.example .env && python scripts/generate_secrets.py --write
$ uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

Open 127.0.0.1:8080 and sign in with the admin login from .env. Run python scripts/seed_demo.py for synthetic demo data.

Going to production? There's Docker Compose for a pilot, a Helm chart for Kubernetes, and Terraform for AWS and Azure. Argus refuses to start in production mode without encryption keys, HTTPS, a write-once audit sink and SSO or two-factor, so an unsafe install can't happen by accident. The full checklist is in [docs/DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/thomasunise/argus/blob/main/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md).

Do it yourself

### Free, forever

Clone it, deploy it, make it yours. Best for teams with security engineers who want to own every line.

*   MIT license: no seats, no usage fees, no vendor lock-in
*   Architecture, threat model, runbooks and a step-by-step go-live guide
*   Issues and contributions welcome on GitHub

Done for you

### I install it and hand it over running

For business owners and lean IT teams who want enterprise-grade protection without hiring a security team to run it. You get the outcome, not the project.

*   Deployed in your own AWS, Azure or Kubernetes account. You own everything
*   Connected to your cloud, logins, code and devices, with alerts in Slack
*   An attack-simulator report showing what you catch today and the gaps we close
*   Rules tuned to your business, and autonomous response proven in shadow mode before it goes live
*   AI gateway and shadow-AI discovery set up so your team's AI use is safe and visible
*   Your team trained on alerts, approvals and the kill switch

What is Argus?
Argus is a free, open-source security operations platform you host yourself. It maps your cloud, identity, code, device, network and Kubernetes assets into one evidence graph, detects attacks including fast, AI-driven ones, uses AI agents to triage and investigate, and fixes problems through an action broker with approvals, dry runs, automatic rollback and a kill switch. It also governs your own company's AI use with an AI gateway and shadow-AI discovery.

Can Argus act on its own? Is that safe?
Only if you turn it on. Autonomous response and autonomous pentesting are off by default and need both a deployment setting and a per-tenant opt-in. Playbooks start in shadow mode, run only reversible actions, are capped per hour, and roll back automatically unless someone keeps the change. The AI agents themselves never execute anything: they investigate with read-only access and can only propose actions. Every change goes through the same broker, and the kill switch stops everything instantly.

Can an attacker trick the AI?
Argus is designed on the assumption that someone will try. Everything an agent reads is wrapped and labelled as untrusted data, and the agent is told that instructions found inside evidence are a sign of an attack. The agents are tested against prompt-injection evaluation suites, and because they cannot execute anything themselves, a tricked agent can at most file a request that still has to pass policy and approval.

What does the attack simulator do to my systems?
Nothing. It replays synthetic attack data in a hidden, isolated sandbox that copies your detection settings. It sends no traffic, runs no tools and touches no real system. Simulated detections can't trigger autonomous response, alerts or findings. You get a coverage report showing which attacks your rules would catch and which would get through.

What is shadow AI, and how does Argus help?
Shadow AI is staff using AI tools the business hasn't approved, often by pasting in customer or company data. Argus finds AI services in your network, cloud and SSO data and keeps an inventory you review. Its AI gateway gives your team approved access to OpenAI and Anthropic models with company-held keys, data-loss rules, budgets, prompt-injection flags and a usage log.

Does it replace my SIEM or EDR?
It works with them. Argus takes events in from thirteen sources, including CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, GuardDuty, Wazuh and CloudTrail, can contain devices through CrowdStrike and SentinelOne, and sends alerts to Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, PagerDuty, email and webhooks. Many teams run it alongside existing tools as the layer that connects the evidence, investigates it and governs the response.

Which AI models does it work with?
Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, local models through Ollama, or none at all. With no model configured, the specialists fall back to deterministic logic, so detection and triage still work. Budgets cap every agent run by steps, tokens, time and cost.

Does my data leave my network?
Argus is self-hosted, so the platform and its data stay in your infrastructure. The only outside calls are the ones you set up: the cloud and identity APIs it collects from, the channels you send alerts to, the public threat-intel feeds, and a model provider i
